En [[fn-derivadas]] se derivaba sin preg: In [[fn-derivadas]] we differentiated without asking whether we could. Almost always you can: polynomials, exponentials, sines and logarithms are differentiable throughout their domain. But there are points where the derivative does not exist, and not because of any computational problem, but because the graph has a corner: it arrives with one gradient and leaves with another. The tool for detecting this is the one-sided limit, now applied to the difference quotient.
Donde más se ve es en las funciones <str: Where it shows up most is in piecewise-defined functions, which is where the exam question falls: “find $a$ and $b$ so that the function is differentiable”. This topic gives the tool —one-sided derivatives— and the recipe for answering it without hesitating.

Durante siglos se dio por hecho que una: For centuries it was taken for granted that a continuous curve had to be differentiable except at a few isolated corners: nobody knew how to draw anything else. In 1872 Karl Weierstrass presented to the Berlin Academy a function, made from an infinite sum of ever tighter cosines, that is continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere: it is corner all the way through. The reaction was one of scandal. Charles Hermite went so far as to write that he turned away in horror from such functions without derivatives. Today we know that, in a precise sense, almost all continuous functions are like this, and that the differentiable ones are the friendly exception.

En ingeniería, «derivable» se dice «suav: In engineering, “differentiable” is called “smooth”, and the difference is felt in the body. A road that goes from a straight line to a circular curve with no transition is continuous but not differentiable in its curvature: it would force you to turn the wheel all at once. That is why motorways and railway lines insert a clothoid between straight and curve, a stretch in which the curvature grows little by little. The same happens in car-body and typeface design: curves are built piecewise, with polynomials, and each join is required to match in value and in derivative, sometimes in the second derivative too, so that the reflection of the light does not break.
